title: Editorial: Generative AI, human authorship and the transformation of scholarly communication
abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools into academic workflows represents a structural transformation in scholarly communication, rather than a transient technological trend (Dwivedi, Malik, Hughes, & Albashrawi, 2024). Similar concerns have been raised in recent editorials in management journals (Arsenyan & Piepenbrink, 2024), which highlight how digital transformation, AI and internationalization pressures are reshaping editorial standards, ethical expectations and scholarly practices (Dwivedi et al., 2023, 2024; Pinochet, Schnaider, & Carvalho, 2025). Unlike conventional software used for editing, formatting or reference management, large language models (LLMs) actively participate in text generation and rhetorical structuring (Brown et al., 2024), thereby challenging long-standing assumptions regarding authorship, intellectual responsibility and research integrity (Dwivedi et al., 2024). This phenomenon reflects what some scholars have characterized as an instant research paradigm, in which GenAI systems potentially conduct multiple steps of the research process simultaneously, raising fundamental questions about scholarly authenticity and human agency in knowledge production.Academic journals are urged to address this new scenario and develop new policies for the use of GenAI tools. Editorial responses to this transformation must engage with the ethical foundations that sustain trust, accountability and transparency in scientific knowledge production (Gatrell, Muzio, Post, & Wickert, 2024). This editorial examines how GenAI reshapes academic writing practices and discusses the ethical boundaries, responsibilities and governance principles required to preserve research integrity. At stake is not only compliance with emerging editorial policies but also the preservation of human authorship as the epistemic condition that sustains interpretation, accountability and legitimacy in scholarly communication.In this context, editorials play a distinctive role in scholarly governance as normative reference points that articulate values, frame ethical expectations and reduce interpretive ambiguity within the scholarly community. By clarifying principles rather than prescribing rigid rules, editorials contribute to a shared ethical understanding among authors, reviewers and editors, addressing the need for discipline-specific guidance, which has become increasingly evident across academic communities (Delios, Li, Schotter, & Vrontis, 2024; Delios, Tung, & Van Witteloostuijn, 2025).Recent reviews of research writing practices indicate that the ethical challenges associated with GenAI are intensified by the absence of harmonized policies across journals and publishers (Okina, 2024). Rather than operating within a coherent normative framework, authors are often confronted with fragmented, ambiguous or incomplete guidance regarding acceptable AI use in academic writing (Ngwenyama & Rowe, 2024). This lack of alignment creates ethical uncertainty and shifts responsibility from institutional governance to individual interpretation, increasing the likelihood of inconsistent disclosure practices and undermining shared standards of academic integrity (Bolaños, Salatino, Osborne, & Motta, 2024).Recent debates in publication ethics have highlighted that the central issue is not whether AI should be used in academic writing, but how, to what extent and under whose responsibility (Dwivedi & Helal, 2026). The presence of hallucinations and AI-generated confident but inaccurate assertions (Thomas, Romasanta, & Pujol Priego, 2026), particularly, threatens the epistemic integrity of academic research, and such errors are especially problematic when AI systems are applied to text analysis and literature synthesis without rigorous human oversight. Evidence from recent systematic and rapid reviews suggests that the ethical dilemma surrounding AI use in academic writing is not whether such tools should be employed but how ethical boundaries are interpreted and operationalized in practice. In the absence of clear editorial guidance, researchers often rely on personal judgment, disciplinary norms or perceived editorial tolerance, leading to uneven ethical reasoning and reinforcing the need for clearer governance structures that support the responsible and transparent use of AI technologies. In this sense, the ethical challenge is not exhausted by asking whether GenAI is present in academic writing. Still, by distinguishing acceptable, sensitive and unacceptable forms of use according to the research stage, the degree of human oversight and the risks posed to intellectual authorship.Viewing it through this lens, ethical engagement with GenAI in academic writing should not be understood as a binary choice between acceptance and prohibition, but as a process of progressive ethical maturation (Delios et al., 2024). What is required, therefore, is not merely procedural compliance but the preservation of cognitive responsibility: human authors must remain the primary agents of framing, interpretation, validation and judgment throughout the scholarly process (Tosi, 2025).As researchers integrate AI tools into scholarly workflows, the central challenge is to develop reflective, responsible and transparent practices that evolve with technological capabilities. Editorial guidance must support this trajectory by encouraging a conscious and proportionate use of AI, rather than treating ethical compliance as a static or purely procedural requirement. This approach acknowledges both the opportunities that AI offers for supporting researchers, particularly non-native English speakers who benefit from language refinement assistance, and the genuine epistemological risks posed by uncritical adoption (Barman, Wood, & Pawlowski, 2024).Good practice guidelines suggest that ethical parameters for AI should not be generic; rather, they should vary with technology and, above all, with the stage of the scientific process in which the tool is applied. This perspective shifts governance away from a binary logic of permit versus prohibit, toward defining proportional uses and safeguards for each phase.AI can contribute to specific tasks in scientific writing, such as identifying research gaps, assisting with content drafting and structuring, extracting data for evidence synthesis, supporting data analysis and interpretation and generating figures and tables (Dwivedi & Helal, 2026). A more precise editorial interpretation also requires recognizing that AI assistance is not ethically uniform. Technical assistance, organizational support and heuristic exploration may be acceptable when explicitly disclosed and critically reviewed. In contrast, substantive substitutions in hypothesis formulation, data interpretation or conclusion writing directly threaten the boundary between assistance and authorship. However, such support must not undermine intellectual authorship: the tool should assist rather than replace the researcher's work, and any AI-assisted text must undergo critical review and content validation, including verification of cited references (Dwivedi & Helal, 2026; Dwivedi et al., 2024).A critical ethical distinction that must be made explicit in editorial policies is the difference between AI-generated and AI-assisted writing. AI-generated writing refers to situations in which AI systems autonomously produce substantial portions of academic texts without meaningful human intellectual control. Such practices raise serious concerns about the attribution of intellectual agency, the erosion of accountability and the misrepresentation of scholarly contributions, particularly when left undisclosed (Gatrell et al., 2024). The fundamental issue is that autonomous AI text generation produces content that, while superficially authoritative, is susceptible to factual errors and misrepresentations (Kulkarni et al., 2024); in extreme cases, it may reference research papers that do not exist or provide incorrect identifiers of unrelated work, presenting what amounts to scholarly hallucinations (Dwivedi et al., 2024).Empirical studies indicate that this distinction is not always consciously perceived by authors (Brown et al., 2024). In many cases, researchers cognitively reframe AI-assisted contributions as extensions of their own thinking, particularly when generative systems are used simultaneously to structure arguments or refine expressions. This cognitive reframing reduces the perceived need for disclosure. It blurs the boundary between assistance and substitution, posing a subtle but significant challenge to traditional notions of authorship and intellectual ownership. Research has demonstrated that human reviewers struggle to reliably distinguish between human-authored and AI-generated abstracts (Kulkarni et al., 2024), further complicating editorial oversight.Ethical analyses consistently emphasize that authorship in scholarly publishing is inextricable from accountability (Hosseini, Rasmussen, & Resnik, 2024). From this perspective, the production of text alone does not constitute authorship unless accompanied by the capacity to assume moral, legal and epistemic responsibility for the content. Because AI systems lack agency, intentionality and accountability, their contributions, regardless of sophistication, cannot meet the normative criteria for scholarly authorship. Scholarly writing is not merely the production of grammatically coherent text; it is an interpretive and moral act through which authors assume responsibility for meaning, evidence and intellectual consequences. Major journal publishers have explicitly articulated this principle; for instance, Science journals have clarified that text generated by ChatGPT or other AI tools cannot be used in scholarly work, nor can such tools produce figures or graphics, and that violations constitute scientific misconduct (Lindebaum & Fleming, 2024).In contrast, AI-assisted writing involves the use of generative systems as supportive tools in human-led research processes (Pinochet, Moreira, Fávero, Santos, & Pardim, 2023). In such cases, AI may contribute to linguistic refinement, structural organization and preliminary drafting (Gatrell et al., 2024). Simultaneously, human authors retain full responsibility for conceptual development, theoretical coherence, methodological rigor and final editorial decisions. From an ethical standpoint, this distinction is fundamental: the acceptability of AI depends less on the technology itself and more on the preservation of human judgment, critical oversight and explicit disclosure (Thomas et al., 2026). This phenomenon has been described as the AI ghostwriter effect (Draxler et al., 2024), referring specifically to AI-assisted authorship rather than fully AI-generated content, in which generative systems support idea formulation or textual organization. At the same time, human authors retain intentionality, judgment and responsibility for the final text, remaining psychologically invisible as external agents. Unlike intentional misconduct, this effect reflects altered perceptions of authorship rather than strategic concealment, suggesting that ethical governance must address not only formal rules but also the cognitive dynamics that shape how AI involvement is interpreted and justified.Beyond individual instances of disclosure failure, a broader systemic risk emerges when GenAI becomes normalized and psychologically invisible in academic writing practices. As AI-mediated structuring, phrasing and ideation become routine, the risk of homogenization in scholarly argumentation, rhetorical patterns and epistemic styles increases. Such normalization may subtly reshape academic discourse, raising concerns not only about authorship and accountability but also about intellectual diversity, originality and the depth of scholarly reasoning. This process may reinforce automation bias and reduce the epistemic vigilance and reflective scrutiny required for rigorous scholarship, especially when scholars begin to rely on fluent AI-generated outputs without sustained verification (Heersmink, 2024; Wong, 2024). Because language models rely on existing literature, heightened attention is needed to avoid the literal reproduction of passages from other authors. This concern is relevant even in the absence of intentional misconduct, as reliance on training corpora may induce textual reuse and unnoticed standardization (Ignjatović & Stevanović, 2023). Recent discussions in the information science and education literature suggest that excessive reliance on GenAI systems may weaken cognitive engagement, critical thinking and creative processes that are central to academic writing (Helal et al., 2025; Kumar & Gunn, 2025; Lindebaum & Fleming, 2024). While generative tools may accelerate drafting and ideation, sustained dependence risks bypassing the reflective, evaluative and iterative stages traditionally associated with scholarly reasoning, raising concerns that extend beyond authorship to the epistemic quality and intellectual depth of academic work.From an editorial standpoint, the ethical acceptability of AI-assisted writing depends on preserving meaningful human control throughout the research process (Thomas et al., 2026). Reviews of editorial policies have indicated that GenAI may be ethically integrated as a support mechanism for language refinement or structural organization, provided that human authors retain responsibility for conceptual framing, methodological decisions and interpretive judgment. This reinforces the principle that ethical evaluation should focus on responsibility and oversight rather than the mere presence of GenAI tools.In practice, transparency is strengthened when authors maintain a minimal provenance record of GenAI assistance (tool name, model/version, date of use and a brief description of prompts or interactions) so that the origins and reliability of AI-assisted passages can be evaluated if questions arise (Herhausen, Ludwig, Abedin, Haque, & De Jong, 2025). Such disclosure is strongest when it identifies not only the tool and model/version used, but also the purpose of use, the degree of intervention and the stage of the manuscript or research process affected, thereby creating conditions for traceability, ethical auditability and informed editorial judgment.This approach acknowledges that prompt engineering and the specific formulation of queries to LLMs significantly influence outputs, making the reproducibility of LLMs essential for scholarly verification (Wobst & Lueg, 2025). For editorial purposes, this differentiation provides a practical and principled framework for evaluating submissions, guiding authors and safeguarding research integrity without impeding legitimate methodological innovations (Herhausen et al., 2025).Within AI-mediated scholarly communication, peer reviewers play a pivotal yet often underarticulated role (Bechky & Davis, 2025). In this evolving landscape, reviewers should be understood not as technological detectors of hidden AI use but as evaluators of coherence, transparency, proportionality and human intellectual responsibility in manuscripts shaped by AI-mediated workflows. Beyond evaluating technical rigor and theoretical contributions, reviewers increasingly serve as interpreters of transparency disclosures and assessors of intellectual coherence in AI-assisted manuscripts. title: NeuroSym-BioCAT: Leveraging Neuro-Symbolic Methods for Biomedical Scholarly Document Categorization and Question Answering
abstract: The growing volume of biomedical scholarly document abstracts presents an increasing challenge in efficiently retrieving accurate and relevant information. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that integrates an optimized topic modelling framework, OVB-LDA, with the BI-POP CMA-ES optimization technique for enhanced scholarly document abstract categorization. Complementing this, we employ the distilled MiniLM model, fine-tuned on domain-specific data, for high-precision answer extraction. Our approach is evaluated across three configurations: scholarly document abstract retrieval, gold-standard scholarly documents abstract, and gold-standard snippets, consistently outperforming established methods such as RYGH and bio-answer finder. Notably, we demonstrate that extracting answers from scholarly documents abstracts alone can yield high accuracy, underscoring the sufficiency of abstracts for many biomedical queries. Despite its compact size, MiniLM exhibits competitive performance, challenging the prevailing notion that only large, resource-intensive models can handle such complex tasks. Our results, validated across various question types and evaluation batches, highlight the robustness and adaptability of our method in real-world biomedical applications. While our approach shows promise, we identify challenges in handling complex list-type questions and inconsistencies in evaluation metrics. Future work will focus on refining the topic model with more extensive domain-specific datasets, further optimizing MiniLM and utilizing large language models (LLM) to improve both precision and efficiency in biomedical question answering.

title: LLMs-based Thematic Analysis of Social Media Deepfakes and its Empirical Parallelism with Deepfake News
venue: Journal of the Association for Information Systems
abstract: This paper discusses deepfakes in social media, a phenomenon that poses a critical challenge to digital trust and information integrity. The deepfakes are improving as technical artifacts, but a cohesive synthesis of the literature is lacking. To address this gap, we conducted a thematic analysis of 109 relevant articles from the literature (2018–2026) that examine the socio-technical implications of deepfakes. Our methodology introduces a rigorous cross-model synthesis through Large Language Models (LLMs). The emerged themes are subsequently mapped onto a corpus of online news articles extracted via GDelt API, using GLDA topic modeling to analogize scholarly findings with real-world insights. The study further identifies critical research gaps in the deepfake domain as it overcommits reactive (forensic detection) and neglects anticipatory (digital literacy) approaches, leading to a Structural Reactivity Gap. This provides the theoretical basis for shifting the deepfake research paradigm from artifact-centric (detecting deepfakes) to agent-centric (understanding deepfakes).
status_reason: LLM thematic synthesis of 109 articles identifies literature research gaps
short_summary: Uses LLMs to thematically analyze 109 deepfake articles and identifies a structural reactivity gap in the literature.
summary: Uses LLMs to thematically synthesise 109 articles on social media deepfakes and maps the themes onto news articles from GDELT with topic modelling. Identifies a structural reactivity gap, where research overemphasises forensic detection and neglects digital literacy. The domain differs from the methods questions of this review.

title: Complementary Vulnerabilities: A Systematic Review Comparing Reasoning Failures in Human and LLM Clinical Decision-Making
abstract: Authors and Affiliations Mohsen Amoei. McGill University, Montreal, Quebec, Canada / Mila - Quebec AI Institute, Montreal, Quebec, Canada Elena Guadagno. Harvey E. Beardmore Division of Pediatric Surgery, The Montreal Children's Hospital, McGill University Health Centre, Montreal, Quebec, Canada Dr Dan Poenaru. Harvey E. Beardmore Division of Pediatric Surgery, The Montreal Children's Hospital, McGill University Health Centre, Montreal, Quebec, Canada Review Question What are the distinct reasoning failure patterns exhibited by human clinicians and large language models (LLMs) in clinical decision-making, how do these failure patterns compare across both systems, and to what extent are they complementary, redundant, or orthogonal? Methods Searches Scientific Literature A medical librarian searched the following databases from January 2018 onward: PubMed, MEDLINE (Ovid), Embase (Ovid), and Scopus. The search employed a three-arm strategy: Search A targeted human clinical reasoning errors using terms related to cognitive biases, diagnostic errors, heuristics, and clinical decision-making failures; Search B targeted LLM clinical reasoning evaluation using terms related to large language models, medical benchmarks, AI hallucination, and reasoning failures; Search C targeted direct human-LLM comparative studies using combined terms from both domains. The search strategy used variations in text words found in the title, abstract or keyword fields, and relevant subject headings to retrieve articles examining reasoning failures in clinical decision-making by either human clinicians or large language models. Grey Literature arXiv was searched for preprints related to LLM clinical reasoning evaluation and AI cognitive biases in healthcare. Forward and backward citation searching (snowballing) will be conducted on all included studies. Conference proceedings and dissertation databases will also be searched. Domain Being Studied This systematic review examines clinical reasoning failures in both human clinicians and large language models performing healthcare decision-making tasks. The domain encompasses diagnostic reasoning, treatment planning, triage, and clinical judgment across all medical specialties. Human reasoning failures include cognitive biases (anchoring, confirmation bias, availability heuristic, premature closure), fatigue-related errors, and experience-dependent failures. LLM reasoning failures include hallucination, prompt sensitivity, context window limitations, training data biases, and non-reproducibility. The review specifically focuses on how and why reasoning fails (failure mechanisms) rather than aggregate performance metrics alone. Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria Studies were included if: (1) the study examined clinical reasoning or diagnostic decision-making by human clinicians (physicians, nurses, medical trainees) or large language models (GPT-4, Med-PaLM, LLaMA, and similar); (2) the study analyzed reasoning failures, errors, cognitive biases, or error mechanisms rather than reporting only accuracy metrics; (3) the study was published in English from January 2018 onward; (4) the study was a primary research article, including empirical studies, benchmark evaluations, randomized experiments, observational studies, cross-sectional surveys, or retrospective analyses; (5) for LLM studies, the system evaluated was a transformer-based large language model. Studies were excluded if: (1) the study focused exclusively on non-clinical AI applications (e.g., administrative, scheduling); (2) the study involved only rule-based or traditional machine learning systems without large language models; (3) the study reported only aggregate accuracy, sensitivity, or specificity without characterizing specific failure types or reasoning mechanisms; (4) the study was an editorial, opinion piece, letter, commentary, or conference abstract without primary data; (5) the study was a case report describing individual diagnostic errors without systematic analysis of reasoning mechanisms. Main Outcome(s) The outcomes of this study will focus on (1) developing a unified taxonomy of clinical reasoning failure types classified as human-unique, LLM-unique, or shared between both systems, with characterization of underlying mechanisms for each failure type; (2) assessing the degree of complementarity between human and LLM reasoning failures, measured by the proportion of failure types that are unique to each system versus shared; (3) determining the prevalence of each failure type reported as the percentage of included studies documenting each reasoning failure; and (4) identifying clinical domains and task types most susceptible to each category of reasoning failure. The unified taxonomy refers to a comprehensive classification framework that maps all identified reasoning failure types into three mutually exclusive categories based on convergent evidence from multiple studies. Complementarity will be assessed by examining whether systems show strengths where the other shows weaknesses, supporting collaborative deployment models. Measures of Effect This review uses qualitative thematic synthesis rather than quantitative meta-analysis. The primary measure is the classification of each reasoning failure type into one of three categories: human-unique, LLM-unique, or shared. For each failure type, prevalence will be reported as the percentage of included studies documenting that failure. For shared failures, mechanistic differences between human and LLM manifestations will be described qualitatively. The degree of complementarity will be expressed as the ratio of unique-to-shared failure types across both systems. Additional Outcome(s) These outcomes will explore the broader implications and applications of the comparative failure taxonomy: Mitigation Strategy Effectiveness: Evaluating the effectiveness of reported mitigation strategies (e.g., structured reasoning prompts, cognitive debiasing techniques, retrieval-augmented generation, chain-of-thought prompting) for reducing reasoning failures in each system, and identifying which strategies show cross-system applicability. Complementarity Thesis Evidence: Assessing evidence for or against the complementarity thesis, specifically whether human and LLM reasoning strengths and weaknesses are inversely correlated, supporting collaborative deployment over substitution models in clinical settings. Domain-Specific Vulnerability Mapping: Mapping failure types to specific clinical specialties and task complexity levels to identify which clinical contexts are most and least suitable for human-AI collaborative decision-making. Data Extraction Data will be extracted using a standardized extraction form. The extraction form will be pilot-tested on a sample of 20 studies to ensure clarity and consistency before proceeding with full data extraction. Extracted data will include: standard bibliographic information (author(s), title, year, journal, DOI/PMID), study design, clinical domain and medical specialty, population characteristics (clinician type, experience level, or LLM model evaluated), reasoning failure types identified with definitions provided by the study authors, failure mechanisms described, prevalence or frequency data where reported, mitigation or debiasing strategies evaluated and their effectiveness, and study limitations. Data will be extracted by one reviewer and verified by a second reviewer. Any disagreements will be resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. A Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) Flow Diagram will be created to detail the number of records identified, screened, included, and excluded, as well as the reasons for exclusions. Strategy for Data Synthesis For this systematic review, data from the included studies will be synthesized using thematic synthesis following the approach described by Thomas and Harden (2008). The synthesis proceeds in three stages: (1) line-by-line coding of extracted data to identify reasoning failure types reported in each study, (2) organization of codes into descriptive themes representing distinct failure categories, and (3) generation of analytical themes through cross-domain comparison of human and LLM failure patterns. Failure types will be classified as human-unique, LLM-unique, or shared based on convergent evidence from multiple studies. For shared failure types, the underlying causal mechanisms in humans versus LLMs will be compared to determine whether failures arise from analogous or distinct processes. Quantitative descriptive statistics will summarize the frequency of each failure type across studies, the distribution of studies across clinical domains, the proportion of studies supporting each taxonomy category, and study quality ratings. No statistical meta-analysis of effect sizes is planned due to the heterogeneity of study designs and outcome measures. Results will be presented using narrative synthesis supplemented by summary tables and a taxonomy visualization diagram. The synthesis findings will be reported in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines. Analysis of Subgroups or Subsets Subgroup analyses will be conducted to explore variation in reasoning failure patterns across the following dimensions: (1) Clinical domain: Comparing failure patterns across specialties (e.g., emergency medicine, oncology, radiology, primary care, surgery) to identify domain-specific vulnerabilities in both human and LLM reasoning. (2) LLM model type: Analyzing whether different model architectures (e.g., GPT-4, Med-PaLM, LLaMA, Claude) exhibit different failure profiles, and whether newer models show improvement on specific failure types. (3) Task complexity: Examining whether failure patterns differ across simple diagnostic tasks (e.g., single-condition identification) versus complex multi-step clinical reasoning (e.g., differential diagnosis w

title: Gifted SLM-as-a-Judge with Attention Steering: Fact-Checking and Detailed Topic Extraction from Academic Literature
abstract: This study proposes the development of an academic domain-specialized Small Language Model (SLM), designed to be used in combination with a general-purpose Large Language Model (LLM), with the objective of constructing a knowledge graph through the highly accurate extraction of detailed technical elements, such as research objectives, methodologies and experimental targets from scholarly articles. The proposed academic domain-specialized SLM is developed through continuous pretraining using collections of survey papers within the target domain and is further optimized to specialize in extracting domain-specific technical elements through attention steering techniques. In the knowledge graph construction process, the SLM is employed as a fact-checking mechanism for outputs generated by a general-purpose LLM. In this paper, we conducted experiments on extracting technical elements in two fields: Fake News Detection in Computer Science and Bibliometrics in Science and Technology Management and confirmed that the proposed academic domain-specialized SLM outperforms general-purpose LLMs in terms of the accuracy, stability and importance of the extracted information. Future work includes constructing a knowledge graph by integrating the proposed SLM with general-purpose LLMs.

short_summary: Continually pretrained small language model acts as fact-checker for general LLM outputs when extracting objectives and methods from academic papers.
summary: Proposes a small academic-domain language model, continually pretrained on survey papers and attention-steered, to fact-check a general LLM's extraction of objectives and methods. Experiments on fake news detection and bibliometrics show it outperforms general LLMs on accuracy, stability and importance. Knowledge graph construction is listed as future work.

title: A Neuro-symbolic Approach for Faceted Search in Digital Libraries
venue: Frontiers in artificial intelligence and applications
abstract: Academic Search Engines (ASEs) are crucial for navigating the vast landscape of scholarly literature. Traditionally, these engines rely on keyword-based search, supplemented by predefined facets encompassing metadata such as research field, publication year, type, authors, and language. However, ASEs are limited in their ability to generate dynamic facets in real-time based on article contents. This limitation impedes the efficient exploration and navigation of large article collections. We propose an approach that addresses this limitation by dynamically generating facets using article abstracts. We introduce three distinct methods for dynamic facet generation: (1) KB2 (based on Knowledge Bases) utilizes two knowledge bases (KB) to extract facet values and their associated facets; (2) KBLLM (based on a Knowledge Base and a Large Language Model) utilizes a KB for extracting facet values and a large language model (LLM) to categorize these values by predicting facets; finally, (3) KBLLMKA (based on a Knowledge Base and a Large Language Model with Knowledge Augmentation) combines KB-spotting with facet-value pair extraction and adds this information as auxiliary data to enhance LLM’s facet prediction capabilities. We evaluated the effectiveness of these methods with a user study, performance evaluation, and comparative analyses, which showed the effectiveness of the approach.

title: From Text to Network: Constructing a Knowledge Graph of Taiwan-Based China Studies Using Generative AI
abstract: Taiwanese China Studies (CS) has developed into a rich, interdisciplinary research field shaped by the unique geopolitical position and long standing academic engagement with Mainland China. This study responds to the growing need to systematically revisit and reorganize decades of Taiwan based CS scholarship by proposing an AI assisted approach that transforms unstructured academic texts into structured, interactive knowledge representations. We apply generative AI (GAI) techniques and large language models (LLMs) to extract and standardize entity relation triples from 1,367 peer reviewed CS articles published between 1996 and 2019. These triples are then visualized through a lightweight D3.js based system, forming the foundation of a domain specific knowledge graph and vector database for the field. This infrastructure allows users to explore conceptual nodes and semantic relationships across the corpus, revealing previously uncharted intellectual trajectories, thematic clusters, and research gaps. By decomposing textual content into graph structured knowledge units, our system enables a paradigm shift from linear text consumption to network based knowledge navigation. In doing so, it enhances scholarly access to CS literature while offering a scalable, data driven alternative to traditional ontology construction. This work not only demonstrates how generative AI can augment area studies and digital humanities but also highlights its potential to support a reimagined scholarly infrastructure for regional knowledge systems.

short_summary: Extracts entity-relation triples from Taiwan China studies articles with LLMs and visualizes a knowledge graph to surface research gaps.

The graph is intended to reveal thematic clusters and research gaps. The abstract gives no quantitative evaluation of extraction accuracy.

title: Repuatix: A Citation Intelligence Framework for Next-Generation Bibliometric Analysis
venue: International Conference on Intelligent Cyber Physical Systems and Internet of Things (ICoICI)
abstract: Traditional bibliometric indicators, such as the impact factor and the h-index, rely heavily on citation counts and assume that all citations carry equal weight. This quantitative focus neglects the qualitative dimensions of scholarly engagement, where citations endorse, dispute, or merely acknowledge prior work. To address this limitation, Repuatix is introduced as a multi-agent citation sentiment-intelligence framework that enriches bibliometric evaluation through analyses of sentiment, intent, certainty, and domain relevance. The framework was implemented using LangGraph, which integrated six sequential agents, namely Fetch, Parse, Relevance, Classify, Reason, and Aggregator, within a directed acyclic graph architecture. The system retrieved metadata and citation records through the Semantic Scholar Application Programming Interface (API), while spaCy and regex-based detection extracted sentence-level citation contexts. MiniLM embeddings and cosine similarity assessed domain relevance, whereas the Large Language Model (LLM) LLaMA3 performed multi-dimensional classification, which enabled structured reasoning across evaluative categories. The framework consolidated the aggregated outputs into interactive reports that provided distribution statistics and representative citation examples. Experimental evaluation demonstrated that Repuatix effectively captured nuanced scholarly reception, particularly through the distinction between favorable and impartial citations, although critical references posed greater classification challenges because of their subtle linguistic characteristics. Repuatix incorporated qualitative citation intelligence into bibliometric analysis and provided transparent, context-aware, and meaningful assessments of scientific impact.

short_summary: Multi-agent LangGraph framework classifies citation sentiment and intent, using embedding relevance filtering before LLaMA3 classification.
summary: Presents Repuatix, a six-agent LangGraph pipeline that retrieves citation records, extracts citation contexts, filters by MiniLM embedding relevance and classifies sentiment, intent and certainty with LLaMA3. Favourable and neutral citations are distinguished well, while critical citations are harder. The evaluation is qualitative in the abstract.

title: Identifying and evaluating emerging scientific trends through temporal n-gram analysis
abstract: Abstract The rapid growth of scientific publishing creates both opportunities and challenges for understanding emerging research trends. Traditional approaches to trend detection, such as citation analyses or latent topic models, often lag behind real developments or lack interpretability. To address these limitations, this study proposes a lightweight and transparent methodology for detecting and evaluating emerging scientific concepts through temporal n -gram analysis. From the OpenAlex corpus of scholarly metadata, n -grams are extracted from titles and abstracts, and aggregated into quarterly frequency series. Bursty dynamics are identified using complementary detection algorithms, including Kleinberg’s state-machine model and a moving average convergence divergence (MACD) approach. Evaluation uses a human-centered framework in which participants judge temporal plots of anonymized n -grams, providing both pairwise comparisons and graded burstiness scores. These judgments are compared with algorithmic rankings, and alignment between large language models (LLMs) and human raters is examined. We further contrast burst dynamics across fast- and slow-evolving subfields and verify the robustness of the approach to corpus-growth effects through a normalization experiment. By integrating scalable temporal analysis and multi-perspective evaluation, this work contributes a framework for monitoring and characterizing the trajectory of emerging research topics. The approach is intended as an interpretable tool for digital libraries, funding agencies, and research analysts seeking to navigate fast-evolving scientific landscapes.
status_reason: Off-topic: temporal n-gram burst detection for emerging trends

title: HySemRAG: A Hybrid Semantic Retrieval-Augmented Generation Framework for Automated Literature Synthesis and Methodological Gap Analysis
abstract: We present HySemRAG, a framework that combines Extract, Transform, Load (ETL) pipelines with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to automate large-scale literature synthesis and identify methodological research gaps. The system addresses limitations in existing RAG architectures through a multi-layered approach: hybrid retrieval combining semantic search, keyword filtering, and knowledge graph traversal; an agentic self-correction framework with iterative quality assurance; and post-hoc citation verification ensuring complete traceability. Our implementation processes scholarly literature through eight integrated stages: multi-source metadata acquisition, asynchronous PDF retrieval, custom document layout analysis using modified Docling architecture, bibliographic management, LLM-based field extraction, topic modeling, semantic unification, and knowledge graph construction. The system creates dual data products - a Neo4j knowledge graph enabling complex relationship queries and Qdrant vector collections supporting semantic search - serving as foundational infrastructure for verifiable information synthesis. Evaluation across 643 observations from 60 testing sessions demonstrates structured field extraction achieving 35.1% higher semantic similarity scores (0.655 $\pm$ 0.178) compared to PDF chunking approaches (0.485 $\pm$ 0.204, p < 0.000001). The agentic quality assurance mechanism achieves 68.3% single-pass success rates with 99.0% citation accuracy in validated responses. Applied to geospatial epidemiology literature on ozone exposure and cardiovascular disease, the system identifies methodological trends and research gaps, demonstrating broad applicability across scientific domains for accelerating evidence synthesis and discovery.

summary: Combines ETL pipelines and hybrid RAG with agentic self-correction to extract fields from literature into Neo4j and Qdrant stores. Structured field extraction beats PDF chunking on semantic similarity, and the system is applied to ozone and cardiovascular literature to identify methodological gaps. Citation accuracy is 99 percent in validated responses.

title: Paper-less FrameWorld
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Scientific research is commonly disseminated through a well-established publication workflow. Researchers conduct a study, prepare a manuscript, submit it for peer review, and publish the accepted work as a static document, typically a PDF. This document becomes the main scholarly object through which the scientific community accesses, evaluates, cites, and discusses the research. Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly involved in this process. Authors use them during research development, literature analysis, writing, revision, and technical exploration. Readers also use LLM-based systems to search the literature, summarize publications, compare methods, extract specific information, and formulate questions about published work. As a consequence, interaction with scientific knowledge is becoming progressively more conversational and query-driven, while the formal publication format remains largely document-based. Paper-less FrameWorld proposes a publication paradigm in which the primary scholarly object is an interactive AI agent. The research is encoded in the agent through its curated knowledge, instructions, sources, research trace, validation rules, and editorial metadata. Readers access the work by interacting directly with this agent and can query its motivation, methodology, assumptions, technical contributions, related work, limitations, open problems, references, and other aspects of the research. The agent-publication is associated with an explicit editorial identity. It identifies its authorship, scope, bibliographic sources, provenance, version, revision history, and validation status. The same framework supports peer review at the level of the agent itself. Reviewers can interrogate the research, examine specific claims, test the consistency of the proposed framework, identify limitations, and formulate requests for clarification or revision. Subsequent releases can incorporate validated revisions while preserving the history and provenance of previous versions. A central component of the paradigm is the distinction between different levels of scientific status. The agent identifies information that belongs to the validated research artifact and distinguishes it from interpretations, derived responses, newly generated content, and material requiring further author validation. Scientific responsibility therefore remains explicitly associated with the authors and with the versioned content that they validate. This interaction-based representation also changes how a reader navigates a scientific contribution. The information traditionally distributed across fixed manuscript sections can be accessed according to the reader's specific questions and level of interest. The resulting scientific object combines the content of the research with its sources, editorial record, validation state, and interaction mechanisms within a single versioned publication. This Zenodo record provides an implementation and experimental instantiation of the Paper-less FrameWorld paradigm. The associated GPT agent constitutes the primary representation of the work and provides interactive access to its scientific content and editorial information.

title: SECite: Analyzing and Summarizing Citations in Software Engineering Literature
venue: Maryland Shared Open Access Repository (USMAI Consortium)
abstract: Identifying the strengths and limitations of a research paper is a core component of any literature review. However, traditional summaries reflect only the authors' self-presented perspective. Analyzing how other researchers discuss and cite the paper can offer a deeper, more practical understanding of its contributions and shortcomings. In this research, we introduce SECite, a novel approach for evaluating scholarly impact through sentiment analysis of citation contexts. We develop a semi-automated pipeline to extract citations referencing nine research papers and apply advanced natural language processing (NLP) techniques with unsupervised machine learning to classify these citation statements as positive or negative. Beyond sentiment classification, we use generative AI to produce sentiment-specific summaries that capture the strengths and limitations of each target paper, derived both from clustered citation groups and from the full text. Our findings reveal meaningful patterns in how the academic community perceives these works, highlighting areas of alignment and divergence between external citation feedback and the authors' own presentation. By integrating citation sentiment analysis with LLM-based summarization, this study provides a comprehensive framework for assessing scholarly contributions.

short_summary: Classifies citation sentiment and uses generative AI to summarize strengths and limitations of nine software engineering papers.

Uses generative AI to summarise the strengths and limitations of each target paper from clustered citation groups and full text. title: Dynamic Programming Optimization of LLM Cascade Ordering for Extracting Sleep Parameters from Mean Sleep Latency Tests
venue: Conference on AI, Science, Engineering, and Technology (AIxSET)
abstract: The objective of this study is to develop and evaluate a scalable natural-language-processing (NLP) pipeline that accurately extracts mean sleep latency (MSL) from Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT) reports in Veterans Health Administration (VHA) records, while minimizing hallucinations and computational cost. We analyzed$\mathbf{1. 3 3}$million VHA clinical notes containing the terms MSLT or multiple sleep latency (1999 - 2025). A logistic-regression classifier using bigram features first identified genuine MSLT notes. Verified notes were processed with a 4-bit-quantized Llama-3.1-8B large language model (LLM); prompts were clinician-guided, and extractions were run at$0.2-1.8$temperature settings ($\Delta=0.1$). To cut missrates without excessive compute, we framed temperature ordering as a dynamic-programming (DP) optimization that, under a predefined cost budget, chooses the cascade of LLM runs that maximizes overall accuracy. Manual annotation of$\mathbf{1, 8 2 5}$randomly sampled notes ($\mathbf{8 4 6}$MSLT, 979 non-MSLT) served as ground truth. The note-identifier achieved mean accuracy$=94.3 {\%}$and AUC$=0.981$(5-fold cross-validation). Filtering reduced hallucinations from$\mathbf{1 0. 8 \%}$to$\mathbf{5. 5 \%}$and misses from 12.8% to 2.4%, raising single-pass extraction accuracy from 73.3% to 87.0%. The DP-optimized cascade further lowered the miss-rate while respecting the cost budget, outperforming any individual-temperature run across all metrics. Clinically, using the 8 -minute MSL cut-off, the final system achieved a sensitivity of 98% and a positive predictive value of 97%.

short_summary: Classifier filters clinical notes, then dynamic programming selects LLM temperature runs under a cost budget to extract mean sleep latency with fewer hallucinations.
summary: Builds a pipeline in which a logistic regression classifier filters clinical notes and a 4-bit Llama-3.1-8B extracts mean sleep latency at several temperatures. Dynamic programming chooses the cascade of runs that maximises accuracy under a cost budget. Filtering cuts hallucinations and misses, and the optimised cascade lowers the miss rate further.

title: Large Language Model Is Not a Good Few-shot Information Extractor, but a Good Reranker for Hard Samples!
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP (Findings of EMNLP)
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have made remarkable strides in various tasks.Whether LLMs are competitive few-shot solvers for information extraction (IE) tasks, however, remains an open problem.In this work, we aim to provide a thorough answer to this question.Through extensive experiments on nine datasets across four IE tasks, we demonstrate that current advanced LLMs consistently exhibit inferior performance, higher latency, and increased budget requirements compared to fine-tuned SLMs under most settings.Therefore, we conclude that LLMs are not effective few-shot information extractors in general 1 .Nonetheless, we illustrate that with appropriate prompting strategies, LLMs can effectively complement SLMs and tackle challenging samples that SLMs struggle with.And moreover, we propose an adaptive filter-thenrerank paradigm to combine the strengths of LLMs and SLMs.In this paradigm, SLMs serve as filters and LLMs serve as rerankers.By prompting LLMs to rerank a small portion of difficult samples identified by SLMs, our preliminary system consistently achieves promising improvements (2.4% F1-gain on average) on various IE tasks, with an acceptable time and cost investment.Our code is available at https://github.com/mayubo2333/LLM-IE.
status_reason: SLM filter then LLM reranks hard samples; LLMs weak few-shot extractors
short_summary: Shows LLMs underperform fine-tuned small models on information extraction, then proposes an SLM-filter, LLM-rerank paradigm that improves F1 at acceptable cost.
summary: Shows that LLMs underperform fine-tuned small models on nine IE datasets across four tasks, with higher latency and cost. Proposes an adaptive filter-then-rerank paradigm in which small models filter and an LLM reranks hard samples, giving about 2.4 F1 gain on average at acceptable cost. Code is released.

title: Calibrate-Then-Delegate: Safety Monitoring with Risk and Budget Guarantees via Model Cascades
abstract: Monitoring LLM safety at scale requires balancing cost and accuracy: a cheap latent-space probe can screen every input, but hard cases should be escalated to a more expensive expert. Existing cascades delegate based on probe uncertainty, but uncertainty is a poor proxy for the utility of an expert call, as it ignores whether the expert would actually improve the prediction. To address this problem, we introduce Calibrate-Then-Delegate (CTD), a model-cascade approach that provides probabilistic guarantees on either computation cost or safety performance while enabling instance-level (streaming) decisions. CTD builds on a novel delegation value (DV) probe, a lightweight model operating on the same internal representations as the safety probe that predicts the benefit of replacing the probe score with the expert score after an expert call. CTD calibrates a threshold on the DV signal using held-out data and multiple hypothesis testing, yielding finite-sample guarantees while optimising the complementary objective. Evaluated on four safety datasets using learned-attention probes, CTD improves over uncertainty-based delegation over much of the budget range, avoids unnecessary expert calls, and extracts positive-value subsets even from groups where the expert score is worse than the probe score on average. Ablations across four probe architectures show that these findings are not specific to any particular architecture.
status_reason: Probe-then-expert model cascade with finite-sample cost guarantees
short_summary: Calibrate-Then-Delegate routes inputs from a cheap safety probe to an expert via a learned delegation-value signal with finite-sample guarantees.
summary: Addresses the cost-accuracy tradeoff in LLM safety monitoring, where a cheap latent probe screens every input and hard cases escalate to an expert model. Proposes Calibrate-Then-Delegate, which uses a learned delegation-value probe and calibrates a threshold with finite-sample guarantees and multiple hypothesis testing. Evaluated on four safety datasets, it improves over uncertainty-based delegation across much of the budget range. The scope is safety monitoring rather than text extraction.
rq_relation: RQ2: probe-then-expert cascade with calibrated cost guarantees, a design reference for cascades

title: LeanContext: Cost-efficient domain-specific question answering using LLMs
abstract: Question-answering (QA) is a significant application of Large Language Models (LLMs), shaping chatbot capabilities across healthcare, education, and customer service. However, widespread LLM integration presents a challenge for small businesses due to the high expenses of LLM API usage. Costs rise rapidly when domain-specific data (context) is used alongside queries for accurate domain-specific LLM responses. Extracting context from domain-specific data is implemented by a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) approach. One option is to summarize the RAG context by using LLMs and reduce the context. However, this can also filter out useful information that is necessary to answer some domain-specific queries. In this paper, we shift from human-oriented summarizers to AI model-friendly summaries. Our approach, LeanContext, efficiently extracts k key sentences from the context that are closely aligned with the query. The choice of k is neither static nor random; we introduce a reinforcement learning technique that dynamically determines k based on the query and context. The rest of the less important sentences are either reduced using a free open-source text reduction method or eliminated. We evaluate LeanContext against several recent query-aware and query-unaware context reduction approaches on prominent datasets (arxiv papers and BBC news articles, NarrativeQA). Despite cost reductions of 37.29% to 67.81%, LeanContext’s ROUGE-1 score decreases only by 1.41% to 2.65% compared to a baseline that retains the entire context (no summarization). LeanContext stands out for its ability to provide precise responses, outperforming competitors by leveraging open-source summarization techniques. Human evaluations of the responses further confirm and validate this superiority. Additionally, if open-source pre-trained LLM-based summarizers are used to reduce context (into human consumable summaries), LeanContext can further modify the reduced context to enhance the accuracy (ROUGE-1 score) by 13.22% to 24.61%.
status_reason: Query-aware sentence selection to cut RAG context cost
short_summary: LeanContext uses RL-chosen key sentence selection before the LLM to cut RAG context cost by 37 to 68 percent with small quality loss.
summary: Targets the cost of RAG-based question answering with LLMs by reducing the domain context sent to the model. Selects k query-aligned key sentences, with k set dynamically by a reinforcement-learning technique, and reduces or drops the remaining sentences. Across arXiv, BBC and NarrativeQA data it cuts cost by 37 to 68 percent with a small ROUGE-1 drop relative to the full context. The work is about question answering rather than research-gap extraction.

title: Knowledge Plugins: Enhancing Large Language Models for Domain-Specific Recommendations
abstract: The significant progress of large language models (LLMs) provides a promising opportunity to build human-like systems for various practical applications. However, when applied to specific task domains, an LLM pre-trained on a general-purpose corpus may exhibit a deficit or inadequacy in two types of domain-specific knowledge. One is a comprehensive set of domain data that is typically large-scale and continuously evolving. The other is specific working patterns of this domain reflected in the data. The absence or inadequacy of such knowledge impacts the performance of the LLM. In this paper, we propose a general paradigm that augments LLMs with DOmain-specific KnowledgE to enhance their performance on practical applications, namely DOKE. This paradigm relies on a domain knowledge extractor, working in three steps: 1) preparing effective knowledge for the task; 2) selecting the knowledge for each specific sample; and 3) expressing the knowledge in an LLM-understandable way. Then, the extracted knowledge is incorporated through prompts, without any computational cost of model fine-tuning. We instantiate the general paradigm on a widespread application, i.e. recommender systems, where critical item attributes and collaborative filtering signals are incorporated. Experimental results demonstrate that DOKE can substantially improve the performance of LLMs in specific domains.
status_reason: Off-topic: domain knowledge prompting for recommender systems

title: Cartography of the Mental Topography of Free-Energy Minimization: A Computational Approach Based on Narrative Trajectory Analysis Using Large Language Models (LLMs)
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: How does the brain protect its beliefs from contradictory facts? Neuroscience answers: through free-energy minimization (FEP, K. Friston), but it does not know the content of these defenses. Linguistics is able to analyze text topics but does not see the dynamics of cognitive tricks. We propose an interdisciplinary method that extracts from text corpora not static topics but dynamic transition graphs: from initial prior beliefs through a point of cognitive friction to final smoothing. Using LLMs in deep reasoning mode, we filter markers of cognitive effort, identify defense operators, and classify them by energy cost (external vs. internal attribution). A rigorous falsifiable hypothesis is advanced concerning a power-law rank distribution of operators, in which low-cost operators (externalization, escapism) monotonically dominate high-cost operators (reflection, restructuring of priors). The method includes a stratified sample across three genres, two-pass semantic compression guided by a taxonomy (Kahneman, A. Freud), and a second-derivative algorithm for identifying the defense core. The project translates qualitative hypotheses into measurable variables and creates the first empirical atlas of collective cognitive algorithms.

title: Enhancing SCADA Alarm Management for Power Grids using Large Language Models
venue: Annual Conference of the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society (IECON)
abstract: SCADA alarm management poses many challenges for power grid control room operators. Vast quantities of information must be managed and filtered by human operators to identify the specific alarm of interest so that system issues can be promptly addressed. The use of knowledge based systems and decision support systems to assist in industrial decision making is well established but comes with heavy cost burdens for development and maintenance. This work demonstrates a possible approach to addressing this cost issue by utilising large language models (LLMs) to parse SCADA alarms and extract information to construct a knowledge base in the form of a knowledge graph. This knowledge base can then be used to construct a decision support system suitable for control room operators to make plain language queries that assist in their problem solving. The decision support approach facilitates better and faster decision making assisting the effective management of electrical distribution networks by control room operators. The case study shown in this work demonstrates that LLMs show promising capacity for knowledge base constructions and have the potential to unlock easy access and insights from large volumes of SCADA alarm data.

title: Automated semantic ontology construction for foresight studies using large language models
abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) enable the automated discovery of semantic structures and emerging signals within text streams, offering an opportunity to redesign foresight workflows into continuous, data-driven systems. This study aims to develop and validate an automated framework for extracting, structuring, and comparing semantic ontologies using LLMs. The paralyzed approach was used for data mining from social media platforms and filtering non-domain data. The key semantic elements, goals and hypernyms corresponded, were extracted using multiple LLM configurations, with a consensus mechanism to provide semantic reliability and minimize hallucination. The extracted elements were embedded in a high-dimensional vector space, clustered iteratively using cosine similarity, and merged hierarchically. Convergence process and structural stability were analyzed using the elbow criterion and similarity metrics. The Proposed approach provides a cost-efficient alternative to traditional expert-based foresight analysis. By integrating LLM-driven semantic extraction with quantitative clustering, it enables the identification of emerging trends, weak signals, and long-term thematic structures. The results highlight the potential of LLM-based semantic modeling as a foundation for automated foresight systems.

title: CascadeFilter: Cost-Efficient Semantic Filtering with Joint Threshold Selection
abstract: Semantic filtering selects records that satisfy a natural-language predicate and is an important operation in data analytics based on large language models (LLMs). Executing an expensive model on every document incurs substantial inference cost. Existing approaches reduce this cost by accepting predictions from cheaper models and forwarding uncertain records to an oracle. Task Cascades further varies document portions and operations, and provides an accuracy-guaranteed extension. However, its threshold calibration follows a prescribed adjustment sequence after cascade assembly, rather than minimizing cost over alternative combinations of stage thresholds. Motivated by this, we propose CascadeFilter, a three-stage semantic filtering method that jointly searches the thresholds for a small language model operating on extracted evidence and full documents, with unresolved records forwarded to the oracle. For a fixed cascade, we formulate threshold selection as minimizing token-aware cost subject to an oracle-relative error constraint, and select the least-cost certified configuration in a pre-specified grid. A finite-population calibration procedure bounds oracle-relative error after selection, using fixed-sequence tests on threshold tracks to allocate the multiple-testing budget. We further combine lexical and dense retrieval, reranking, and neighborhood-supported confidence to improve evidence extraction and routing. These components enhance the cascade while leaving its certification interface unchanged. Across six datasets and 13 evaluation settings, the reported results have the highest benchmark accuracy and macro-averaged F1 score in 12 settings each. These comparisons describe the reported operating points; the accuracy guarantee concerns agreement with the oracle.
status_reason: Cascade of small LLM and oracle for semantic filtering, cost-accuracy
short_summary: CascadeFilter jointly tunes thresholds across a small-LLM cascade on evidence and full documents, minimizing token cost under certified oracle-relative error.
summary: Addresses cost-efficient semantic filtering with LLMs, where a small model handles most records and uncertain ones are forwarded to an oracle. Proposes a three-stage cascade that jointly searches thresholds for a small LLM operating on extracted evidence and on full documents, minimizing token-aware cost under an oracle-relative error constraint. Uses finite-population calibration with fixed-sequence tests for the guarantee. Reports the highest accuracy in 12 of 13 evaluation settings across six datasets; the guarantee concerns agreement with the oracle.

title: Data Selection for Fine-tuning Large Language Models Using Transferred Shapley Values
venue: Proceedings of the conference - Association for Computational Linguistics. Meeting
abstract: Although Shapley values have been shown to be highly effective for identifying harmful training instances, dataset size and model complexity constraints limit the ability to apply Shapleybased data valuation to fine-tuning large pretrained language models.To address this, we propose TS-DSHAPLEY, an algorithm that reduces computational cost of Shapley-based data valuation through: 1) an efficient samplingbased method that aggregates Shapley values computed from subsets for valuation of the entire training set, and 2) a value transfer method that leverages value information extracted from a simple classifier trained using representations from the target language model.Our experiments applying TS-DSHAPLEY to select data for fine-tuning BERT-based language models on benchmark natural language understanding (NLU) datasets show that TS-DSHAPLEY outperforms existing data selection methods.Further, TS-DSHAPLEY can filter fine-tuning data to increase language model performance compared to training with the full fine-tuning dataset.

title: Ontology-Driven Adaptive Learning Environment Using Large Language Models for Educational Knowledge Extraction
abstract: Enriching educational ontologies automatically from low-resource-language text remains an unsolved integration problem: conventional large language model (LLM)-to-knowledge-graph pipelines require a vocabulary-alignment step and lack hallucination control at the commit boundary. This study removes both bottlenecks and tests whether the resulting ontology can drive measurable learning gains. The core idea is schema co-design: the JSON schema constraining LLM output is the OWL T-box of the target ontology, so extracted records are directly populatable and no alignment step is needed; a literal-presence filter rejects entities absent from the source text before commit, the HermiT reasoner verifies consistency, and Kazakh, Russian and English labels are generated in a single follow-up call. The pipeline (Python 3.9, OWLready2) was benchmarked on 90 Kazakh paragraphs across GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Gemini 1.5 Pro, and the resulting adaptive textbook was evaluated quasi-experimentally with 65 Grade 6 students (control n = 32, experimental n = 33) in two Astana schools over 16 weeks. Of 312 source chunks, 271 (86.9%) survived the full validation chain, yielding 1,847 OWL individuals, 2,931 object-property assertions and 6,512 data-property annotations across 47 classes; the literal-presence filter intercepted 5.2% of validated responses and the reasoner a further 1.1%. Extraction F1 reached 0.89 (GPT-4o), 0.87 (Claude) and 0.86 (Gemini), with hallucination rates of 4.9–8.3%; the one-time corpus build cost USD 3.47–9.64, with zero marginal LLM cost per learner. The experimental group outperformed controls on task accuracy (+19.4 points, d = 2.30), repeated errors (−53.6%, d = 1.85) and sessions to mastery (−34.3%, d = 1.50), all p < 0.001 under Bonferroni correction. The novelty lies in making the ontology T-box itself the extraction schema, combined with pre-commit literal grounding, validated in a real low-resource classroom deployment.

short_summary: Kazakh educational ontology pipeline with schema-as-T-box extraction, literal-presence filtering and reasoner checks, plus a classroom study.
summary: Builds an educational ontology from Kazakh text by using an LLM extraction schema that is the ontology T-box, with a literal-presence filter and a HermiT reasoner check. Benchmarks GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Gemini 1.5 Pro on 90 paragraphs, reporting extraction F1 of 0.86 to 0.89. A 65-student quasi-experiment reports learning gains. Relevance is limited to the pre-commit literal-grounding filter as a hallucination control.

title: Narrative Shift Detection: A Hybrid Approach of Dynamic Topic Models and Large Language Models
abstract: With rapidly evolving media narratives, it has become increasingly critical to not just extract narratives from a given corpus but rather investigate, how they develop over time. While popular narrative extraction methods such as Large Language Models do well in capturing typical narrative elements or even the complex structure of a narrative, applying them to an entire corpus comes with obstacles, such as a high financial or computational cost. We propose a combination of the language understanding capabilities of Large Language Models with the large scale applicability of topic models to dynamically model narrative shifts across time using the Narrative Policy Framework. We apply a topic model and a corresponding change point detection method to find changes that concern a specific topic of interest. Using this model, we filter our corpus for documents that are particularly representative of that change and feed them into a Large Language Model that interprets the change that happened in an automated fashion and distinguishes between content and narrative shifts. We employ our pipeline on a corpus of The Wall Street Journal news paper articles from 2009 to 2023. Our findings indicate that a Large Language Model can efficiently extract a narrative shift if one exists at a given point in time, but does not perform as well when having to decide whether a shift in content or a narrative shift took place.

short_summary: Topic models and change-point detection filter representative documents, then an LLM interprets narrative shifts in 2009 to 2023 WSJ news.
summary: Detects narrative shifts in news corpora by combining dynamic topic models with change-point detection to select representative documents. An LLM then interprets each detected shift and separates content changes from narrative changes. Applied to Wall Street Journal articles from 2009 to 2023, the LLM finds shifts efficiently when they exist but performs worse at classifying the shift type. The domain is news rather than scientific text.

title: Evaluating Large Language Model News Sentiment in Finance under Liquidity and Market Frictions
abstract: This paper studies whether large language models can extract useful sentiment signals from firm-specific financial news when evaluation accounts for realistic market frictions.Many financial NLP studies report strong offline prediction results, but these do not always show whether model outputs remain useful once trading constraints are imposed.I address this gap by evaluating sentiment models through classification performance, return predictability, and implementable portfolio performance.The analysis links Refinitiv News Analytics to CRSP and begins with 3,129,924 U.S. news items published between January 1, 2010 and January 30, 2026.Filtering retains single-firm stories, removes redundant coverage using a five-day cosine-similarity novelty screen, and restricts the sample to tradable stocks with positive bid and ask quotes, minimum share and dollar volume thresholds, quoted spreads below 20%, and available Amihud illiquidity ratios and Kyle's lambda estimates.The final sample contains 973,481 tradable news items linked to 3,452 firms.I compare six sentiment approaches: LLaMA-3, OPT, RoBERTa, BERT, FinBERT, and the Loughran-McDonald dictionary.LLaMA-3 achieves the strongest classification performance with 78.2% accuracy and produces the largest predictive coefficients in panel regressions.Daily rebalanced long-short portfolios with a 5 bps trading cost show that the LLaMA-3 strategy earns a cumulative return of approximately 180% from June 2024 to January 2026, followed by OPT with 155% and RoBERTa with 120%, while the dictionarybased strategy loses 9%.The results show that evaluation becomes more informative when financial NLP models are assessed beyond offline accuracy and under realistic deployment constraints.High-capacity language models retain economically meaningful predictive content under market frictions, whereas simpler lexicon-based methods do not.

title: Automated Classification of Offshore Production Units Maintenance Notes Using Machine Learning and Large Language Models
abstract: Abstract Regular maintenance is vital for offshore rig safety and cost-efficiency, requiring careful planning to prevent downtime. Thousands of procedures occur yearly, posing challenges in resource allocation and scheduling. A key issue is identifying tasks that require production halts versus those that can proceed safely, as misclassification may cause downtime or safety risks. This paper explores using machine learning and large language models (LLMs) to automate maintenance task classification based on historical records. Methods, Procedures, Process The methodology involved a structured data pipeline to unify and prepare maintenance records for machine learning classification. Maintenance notes and tactical portfolios were consolidated into a single dataset through filtering, renaming, and type conversion. A Random Forest classifier was developed using thousands of offshore maintenance records. LLMs were employed to extract relevant terms and contextual features from maintenance notes to improve classification performance. These features were integrated into the classifier to distinguish tasks requiring production stops from those that did not. Model performance was evaluated using accuracy, precision, and F-score, and compared to traditional feature engineering methods. Results, Observations, Conclusions The classification model achieved 92% accuracy, with precision and F-score also reaching 92%, demonstrating robustness in real-world scenarios. Integrating LLMs significantly improved reliability compared to conventional text-based feature extraction. By automating classification, the system enables more informed decision-making, optimizing scheduling and minimizing unnecessary halts, thereby reducing safety risks. These advancements enhance operational efficiency and cost-effectiveness. The study also highlights the potential of AI-driven approaches in addressing offshore maintenance challenges, particularly logistical coordination and resource allocation. The system processes maintenance notes in two ways: through integration with proprietary systems accessing relevant databases, and through manual uploading of data extracted from CMMS. This dual data ingestion ensures comprehensive coverage, further supporting the model's efficacy in improving decision-making and efficiency in offshore maintenance. Novel/Additive Information This research introduces an innovative application of LLMs for offshore maintenance classification, outperforming traditional methods. It integrates AI to improve maintenance planning and resource allocation, contributing to petroleum industry efficiency. This work builds on the Petrobras Conexões para Inovação project, where machine learning was tested to classify maintenance notes from three offshore platforms.

title: Prompt Engineering for Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Status Extraction: Comparing Large Language Model Techniques
abstract: PURPOSE Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status is critical for cancer patient management, yet it is often documented only in unstructured clinical notes. This study compares several approaches to extract ECOG status from oncology notes, focusing on advanced prompting techniques for large language models (LLMs). METHODS We evaluated four ECOG extraction approaches on unstructured clinical notes from patients with non–small cell lung cancer, multiple myeloma, or ovarian cancer (2017-2021). The approaches were a rule-based natural language processing algorithm, simple LLM prompting, and two advanced prompts (chain-of-thought and Double Filtering) using a domain-tuned LLM (LLAMAv3.2). Performance was measured on a binary outcome (any ECOG documented v none) and a three-class outcome (ECOG 0-1 v ≥2 v none) and via an adapted QUEST questionnaire for human evaluation. RESULTS Both CoT and double filtering technique (DFT) achieved 94% accuracy, outperforming the rule-based method (91%) and simple prompting (86%). DFT had the highest specificity (0.91) and positive predictive value (PPV; 0.93), whereas CoT attained the highest sensitivity (0.98). In the QUEST evaluation, DFT and CoT scored higher on output quality, reasoning, bias reduction, and user satisfaction than the simple prompt. DFT received the top satisfaction rating. In the three-class analysis, DFT and CoT again performed best (accuracy 0.91 v 0.87) and DFT was most sensitive for ECOG ≥2 cases. Estimates for ECOG ≥2 remained imprecise because of the small sample (n = 20). All methods sometimes hallucinated ECOG status. CONCLUSION Advanced LLM prompting improved ECOG extraction over basic methods. DFT and CoT each showed specific strengths (DFT had higher PPV and user satisfaction; CoT achieved higher sensitivity). These approaches appear to be generalizable across cancer types. Key implementation considerations include computational cost and human oversight. Overall, advanced prompting can standardize ECOG documentation, accelerate patient cohort identification, and inform personalized treatment planning.
status_reason: Double-filtering LLM prompting vs simple prompting for clinical extraction
short_summary: Compares rule-based, simple, chain-of-thought and Double Filtering LLM prompting for ECOG status extraction; filtering reaches 94 percent accuracy.
summary: Compares rule-based NLP, simple LLM prompting, chain-of-thought and Double Filtering for extracting ECOG performance status from oncology notes, using a domain-tuned Llama 3.2. Double Filtering and chain-of-thought each reach 94 percent accuracy, versus 86 percent for simple prompting. The class with ECOG 2 or above has only 20 cases, so estimates are imprecise, and all methods sometimes hallucinate.
